title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
gist: Hugging Face let a coding agent with an inference-optimisation skill tune Inkling 2 Mini (looped MoE, ~26B total/3B active) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, raising single-user decode from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) and 8-user throughput from ~570 to 716 tok/s via vLLM nightly plus DSpark speculative decoding. The result sits at ~95% of the bandwidth ceiling, and the config was deployed as an Inference Endpoint.

insights.claim: Inkling 2 Mini has ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs and a 1M-token context, and leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Small open MoE models are getting competitive for coding/tool use on modest hardware — pressure on closed API pricing.
insights.locator: Inkling 2 Mini came out last week

insights.claim: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 run three times, so each token passes through 48 layers; it ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 with a bundled DSpark drafter.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Looped-layer architectures trade parameter memory for compute — a design trend relevant to edge inference.
insights.quote: a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times

insights.claim: vLLM and SGLang support Inkling 2 Mini on nightly builds, but published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Software support lags on workstation-class NVIDIA GPUs; datacenter Blackwell gets first-class recipes.

insights.claim: A coding agent given Hugging Face's inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI and HF Jobs ran 46 valid benchmark runs in an afternoon, lifting single-user decode from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) and 8-user throughput from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%).
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Autonomous agents can now do production inference tuning — a productivity lever for ML ops and a selling point for HF Jobs.

insights.claim: The tuned 190.6 tok/s beat the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Agent-tuned configs can exceed community best-known results.

insights.claim: The skill's protocol: estimate hardware ceilings first, change one variable at a time bracketed by control runs (control → candidate → control), log every run including dead ends, and pass long-context, concurrency and greedy-equivalence gates before declaring a winner.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Reusable rigorous benchmarking methodology that guards against noise-driven false wins.

insights.claim: The HF rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint, both priced at $2.75/h, so Job benchmark numbers transfer directly to deployment.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Pricing benchmark for single-GPU inference hosting on Hugging Face.

insights.claim: When flags were undocumented, the agent ran cheap CPU Jobs to grep the installed engine packages, discovering SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Agents can reverse-engineer undocumented config surfaces — documentation gaps matter less.
insights.locator: CPU Jobs for reading engine source.

insights.claim: Switching from SGLang to vLLM nightly gave +15% without speculation (136 → 157 tok/s), and enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling added +21% (157 → 190.6 tok/s).
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: vLLM held an edge over SGLang on this sm120 GPU — engine choice is a first-order performance lever.
insights.locator: All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly

insights.claim: Greedy draft sampling cut vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 versus probabilistic sampling, and SGLang's greedy-draft setting cost 9%.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Speculative decoding settings must match sampling temperature to realize gains.

insights.claim: Across identical speculative runs vLLM varied within 0.4% while SGLang swung ±4.5%, enough to make an SGLang optimization flag look like a +4% win before repeat controls ruled it out.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Run-to-run variance can masquerade as optimization gains; demand repeated controls in vendor benchmarks.

insights.claim: The team avoided output-altering rejection-sampling methods ('fly' and 'synthetic') to keep a strictly lossless speedup; greedy outputs were 6/6 byte-identical with and without DSpark speculation.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Lossless speculative decoding is production-safe; quality is not traded for speed.

insights.claim: On the RTX PRO 6000 (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth), plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts and ~0.9 GB for the LM head per token across 48 layer visits, implying a single-user ceiling of ~256 tok/s; vLLM without speculation reached 61% of it, limited mostly by kernel launch latency.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Memory bandwidth, not FLOPS, bounds single-user LLM decode — favors high-bandwidth GPUs.

insights.claim: Speculative decoding on an MoE verifying 8 positions activates the union of their routed experts, reading ~40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%, which lowers the bandwidth ceiling to ~201 tok/s at ~2.3 accepted tokens per step.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Speculative decoding gains are structurally smaller on MoE models — a key consideration for MoE serving economics.
insights.quote: Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE.
insights.locator: Speculative decoding changes the memory math

insights.claim: At 190.6 tok/s vLLM + DSpark is at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further gains require a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path touching fewer experts per layer.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Next inference gains on this class come from better drafters/MoE-aware verification, not flag tuning.
insights.quote: further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go

insights.claim: vLLM v0.34.0 raised the default --gpu-memory-utilization from 0.92 to 1.0, which caused the KV cache to claim remaining VRAM and OOM the DSpark drafter's 5 GiB allocation; setting it to 0.85 plus capping max-model-len at 262144 fixed startup on 96 GB.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Engine default changes can silently break speculative-decoding deployments — pin versions.
insights.locator: Hidden OOM errors in vLLM logs.

insights.claim: Triton JIT compilation during timed requests made vLLM's first 4K prefill report 202 tok/s instead of ~20K, requiring unmeasured warmups across prompt lengths and concurrency.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Unwarmed benchmarks badly understate prefill throughput — scrutinize published numbers.

insights.claim: The pinned vLLM nightly config passed needle retrieval 3/3 at ~95% context (249,970 tokens) and a concurrent 4×~58K-token soak, and the deployed Inference Endpoint measured 194.9 tok/s single-user over the internet.
insights.speaker: Niels Rogge
insights.so_what: Production-validated config; long-context quality holds under the tuned setup.
